title: Scripture, Tradition and Who Interprets
lead: Where does the church find God's word, and who has the right to explain it? All Christians hold the Bible to be God's word, but they differ on how it relates to the teaching handed down in the church, and on whether the church's leaders, the creeds, or each believer reading with the Spirit has the final say.

sections.h: Handing down and explaining in the Bible
sections.b: Moses told Israel not to add to or take away from his commands (Deuteronomy 4:2), and said that "what has been made known is for us and our children for all time" (Deuteronomy 29:29). After the exile the Levites explained the law so that the people understood what was read (Nehemiah 8:7–8). Jesus criticized those who set aside God's command for human tradition (Mark 7:8–13). Yet Paul tells the Thessalonians to hold to the traditions they were taught, whether by word or by letter (2 Thessalonians 2:15), and passes on what he received (1 Corinthians 11:2; 1 Corinthians 15:3). Jude urges believers to fight for "the faith that was handed down to the saints once for all" (Jude 1:3). Scripture is "God-breathed" and useful for teaching (2 Timothy 3:16–17), but some parts are hard to understand (2 Peter 3:16), and the Ethiopian official asked how he could understand unless someone guided him (Acts 8:30–31). The apostles and elders met together to settle a dispute (Acts 15).

sections.b: Catholic teaching holds that Scripture and Tradition flow from the same source and together form one deposit of faith. The task of giving the authentic interpretation belongs to the church's teaching office, the Magisterium, the pope and the bishops in union with him, which is not above God's word but serves it (Dei Verbum 9–10). Orthodox Christians see Scripture as the heart of a living Tradition that also includes the creeds, the seven ecumenical councils, the church fathers and the liturgy; the whole church, guided by the Holy Spirit, receives and guards the faith. Jewish tradition has a parallel idea: the Oral Torah, which the Mishnah says Moses received at Sinai and handed down along with the written law.

The Reformers taught sola scriptura, "Scripture alone": the Bible is the only infallible rule for faith, and every church teaching must be tested by it. This did not mean ignoring tradition. Lutherans, Reformed and Anglicans keep the ancient creeds as faithful summaries of Scripture, and the Westminster Confession says Scripture is its own best interpreter, the clearer passages explaining the harder ones. Methodists speak of Scripture as primary, read with tradition, reason and experience. Many Baptists, Anabaptists and Restorationists stress each believer's right to read the Bible, some with the motto "No creed but the Bible." Quakers give first place to the inward light of Christ, by which Scripture is understood. Latter-day Saints accept further books of scripture and living prophets.

common: Christians agree that the Bible is God's word and that the church must read it faithfully.
uncommon: Some Protestants practice "solo scriptura," rejecting creeds and the church's historic reading altogether, a view many Reformers would not have shared.
